Clinical Reference · Biliary Infection

Acute Cholecystitis & Cholangitis

On this page
Two diseases of one obstructed system: acute cholecystitis is a blocked cystic duct inflaming the gallbladder; acute cholangitis is a blocked common bile duct with an infected, pressurized biliary tree that seeds the blood — a drainage emergency until proven otherwise.
Cystic duct → cholecystitis CBD stone → cholangitis Cholecystitis: antibiotics + early lap chole <72 h Cholangitis: antibiotics + biliary drainage Grade III cholangitis mortality ~10–20% Grading = Tokyo Guidelines 2018
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — one obstructed plumbing system, two very different diseases

Both diseases start with the same substrate — gallstones — but the disease you get depends entirely on where the stone lodges. The biliary tree is a plumbing system: bile made in the liver drains down the common hepatic duct, the gallbladder hangs off to the side on the cystic duct as a storage reservoir, and everything empties through the common bile duct (CBD) into the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater. Block the side branch (cystic duct) and you inflame the gallbladder — acute cholecystitis. Block the main drain (CBD) and you pressurize and infect the entire tree — acute cholangitis.

Acute cholecystitis — a blocked cystic duct

A stone impacts in the gallbladder neck or Hartmann's pouch, obstructing the cystic duct. The gallbladder keeps secreting mucus and can't empty, so it distends; rising wall tension compresses the mucosal blood supply → ischemia. Retained bile salts and lysolecithin chemically injure the mucosa, and prostaglandins (I₂ and E₂) drive the inflammatory secretion and pain. This first phase is a chemical/ischemic inflammation — which is why in the first day or two bile cultures are often sterile. Secondary bacterial infection (E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus) then supervenes in roughly a third to half of cases, and if the wall ischemia goes far enough you get the dangerous variants: gangrenous, emphysematous (gas-forming organisms in a poorly perfused wall, classically in diabetics), empyema, and perforation. About 90–95% of acute cholecystitis is calculous (stone-driven); the remaining acalculous cholecystitis is a disease of the critically ill (see Complications).

Acute cholangitis — a blocked, infected common bile duct

Here a stone (or a stricture, tumor, or clogged stent) obstructs the CBD. Bile above the blockage stagnates and becomes colonized with gut bacteria. The key event is pressure: normal biliary pressure is ~7–10 cmH₂O, but an obstructed duct climbs past ~20–25 cmH₂O, and at that pressure the tight junctions between cholangiocytes fail — infected bile refluxes directly into the hepatic sinusoids and lymphatics (cholangiovenous and cholangiolymphatic reflux). Bacteria and endotoxin pour straight into the bloodstream, so cholangitis is fundamentally a bacteremia/sepsis syndrome, not just a local infection. This is the single most important concept in the whole guide: you cannot sterilize a duct that is still under pressure — the treatment is to relieve the pressure (drainage), and antibiotics only buy you time.

Think of the biliary tree as a house's plumbing. The gallbladder is a storage tank on a side pipe; cap that side pipe with a stone and the tank swells, its walls starve, and it gets angry — that's cholecystitis, and the fix is to take out the ruined tank. The common bile duct is the main sewer line; jam it and sewage backs up under pressure until it forces its way into the clean water supply (your bloodstream) — that's cholangitis, and no amount of disinfectant poured in the top helps until a plumber physically opens the drain.
Biliary anatomy — the gallbladder drains via the cystic duct into the common bile duct, which joins the pancreatic duct at the ampulla. A cystic-duct stone → cholecystitis; a common-bile-duct stone → cholangitis.
Illustration: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
The substrate — mixed gallstones. ~10–15% of adults have gallstones; most stay silent, but a stone that migrates decides which disease you get.
Photo: George Chernilevsky · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
The same stone, two destinations: the cystic duct fork drives the inflammation/surgery disease; the common-bile-duct fork drives the pressure/sepsis/drainage disease.
Every therapy in this guide maps onto this cascade. Antibiotics cover the translocated enteric flora (gram-negatives + anaerobes ± Enterococcus) — they treat the infection step but not the obstruction. Cholecystectomy removes the obstructed, inflamed gallbladder at the source. ERCP / biliary drainage is the definitive move for cholangitis because it relieves the intraductal pressure that is driving the bacteremia. Percutaneous cholecystostomy decompresses the gallbladder when a patient is too sick for surgery. NSAIDs blunt the prostaglandin-mediated inflammation and pain of early biliary colic/cholecystitis. Match each intervention to the step it interrupts and none of the management feels arbitrary.

Diagnosis & severity grading (TG18)

🗂️

The Tokyo Guidelines 2018 — the language that drives every decision

The Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) give both a diagnostic triad and a severity grade (I–III) for each disease, and the grade dictates timing of surgery/drainage and antibiotic breadth. Learn these — they are the vocabulary of every biliary consult.

Diagnostic criteria

PartAcute cholecystitis (Yokoe TG18)Acute cholangitis (Kiriyama TG18)
A — Local / systemic inflammationA. Local signs: Murphy's sign, RUQ mass/pain/tendernessA. Systemic inflammation: fever >38 °C and/or shaking chills; lab evidence (WBC <4 or >10 ×10³/mm³, CRP ≥1 mg/dL)
B — Systemic / cholestasisB. Systemic signs: fever, ↑CRP, ↑WBCB. Cholestasis: jaundice (total bilirubin ≥2 mg/dL); abnormal LFTs (ALP, γGTP, AST, ALT >1.5× ULN)
C — ImagingC. Imaging findings characteristic of acute cholecystitis (US wall thickening, distension, stone/debris, sonographic Murphy)C. Biliary dilatation, or evidence of the cause (stone, stricture, stent) on imaging
SuspectedOne item in A + one item in BOne item in A + one item in B or C
DefiniteOne item in A + one in B + COne item in A + one in B + one in C

Severity grade — and what it triggers

Both diseases share the same Grade III organ-dysfunction definition; the Grade II criteria differ (below). Grade escalates timing of drainage and level of care.
GradeAcute cholecystitis (TG18)Acute cholangitis (TG18)
III (Severe)Same for both — onset of dysfunction in ≥1 organ/system: Cardiovascular (hypotension needing dopamine ≥5 µg/kg/min or any norepinephrine) · Neurological (↓consciousness) · Respiratory (PaO₂/FiO₂ <300) · Renal (oliguria or creatinine >2.0 mg/dL) · Hepatic (PT-INR >1.5) · Hematological (platelets <100,000/mm³)
II (Moderate)Any ONE of: WBC >18,000/mm³ · palpable tender RUQ mass · duration >72 h · marked local inflammation (gangrenous, emphysematous, pericholecystic/hepatic abscess, biliary peritonitis)Any TWO of: WBC >12,000 or <4,000/mm³ · fever ≥39 °C · age ≥75 · total bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL · albumin <0.7× lower limit of normal
I (Mild)Meets neither Grade III nor Grade II (mild inflammation, healthy patient)Meets neither Grade III nor Grade II
The grade is dynamic — re-grade after resuscitation. A patient who is hypotensive on arrival (Grade III) but whose pressure normalizes with a fluid bolus may functionally behave like Grade II; conversely a "Grade I" who isn't improving at 24 h needs the same urgent drainage as Grade II. Use the grade to trigger action, not to lock the patient into a box. Build the exact grade with the interactive calculators (cholecystitis → Wards; cholangitis → ICU).

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Cholecystitis is persistent RUQ pain in someone who looks uncomfortable but not usually septic; cholangitis is the same RUQ pain plus the fingerprints of a bloodstream infection — fever and jaundice (Charcot), and in severe cases hypotension and confusion (Reynolds). Note how low the sensitivity of the classic findings is: absence of fever does not exclude cholecystitis, and the full Charcot triad is present in only about a quarter of cholangitis.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Cholecystitis: RUQ / epigastric pain, often >4–6 h (vs self-limited biliary colic)~80–90%Sustained cystic-duct obstruction → gallbladder distension and wall inflammation irritating the parietal peritoneum. Unlike biliary colic (waxes/wanes over <6 h), cholecystitis pain is constant and prolonged.
Nausea / vomiting / anorexia~60–70%Visceral afferent activation and reflex ileus from the inflamed gallbladder.
Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation)~60–65% sensThe descending inflamed gallbladder strikes the examining hand → the patient catches their breath. Clinical Murphy's ~65% sensitive/~87% specific; sonographic Murphy's is ~90% sens/spec and more reliable. Less sensitive in the elderly.
Fever (cholecystitis)~30–35%Surprisingly uncommon — early cholecystitis is a chemical inflammation, so most patients are afebrile. A high fever/rigors should make you think secondary infection, gangrene, or that this is actually cholangitis.
Pain radiating to right scapula / shoulder~20–30%Referred pain via shared dermatomal/phrenic innervation of the gallbladder and diaphragm (Boas' sign = right subscapular hyperesthesia).
Cholangitis: fever~80–90%Direct bacteremia/endotoxemia from cholangiovenous reflux — fever is the rule in cholangitis (vs the exception in cholecystitis).
Abdominal pain (cholangitis)~70–80%Ductal distension and inflammation; often less localized/severe than cholecystitis.
Jaundice (cholangitis)~60–70%CBD obstruction backs conjugated bilirubin into the blood. Its presence is what completes Charcot's triad and points to the duct, not the gallbladder.
Charcot triad (fever + RUQ pain + jaundice)~15–26%All three together is specific (~96%) but insensitive (~26%) — its absence never rules out cholangitis. Modern series show most cholangitis presents incomplete.
Reynolds pentad (Charcot + hypotension + confusion)<5–10%Adds septic shock + encephalopathy — the Grade III end of the spectrum. Rare but a mortality flag demanding emergent drainage.
Altered mental status / hypotension (elderly, diabetic)variableOlder and diabetic patients present atypically — sepsis or delirium without localizing pain. Keep biliary sepsis on the differential for any unexplained gram-negative bacteremia.
Read the patternPersistent RUQ pain + positive Murphy + minimal/no fever → think cholecystitis. RUQ pain + fever + jaundice (± hypotension/confusion) → think cholangitis and start planning drainage. The bilirubin and the duct diameter are the pivot: a normal/near-normal bilirubin with a non-dilated CBD favors cholecystitis; a rising bilirubin with a dilated CBD says the stone is in the main duct.
🪛

Imaging — what to order, what it shows, and the order it appears

Right-upper-quadrant ultrasound is first-line for both diseases (ACR Appropriateness Criteria) — no radiation, bedside-available, and it answers the two key questions: are there stones, and is the duct dilated. Its limits define when you escalate to HIDA, CT, MRCP, or EUS.

ModalityTest characteristics / roleKey findings & thresholds
RUQ ultrasound (first-line)For cholecystitis ~81% sens / ~83% spec (Kiewiet meta-analysis). Operator-dependent; best single first test.GB wall >3 mm, distension (>4 cm short axis / >8 cm long), pericholecystic fluid, stones/sludge, sonographic Murphy's. For cholangitis: CBD dilatation >6 mm (add ~1 mm/decade over 60; up to ~10 mm post-cholecystectomy) ± a visible stone.
HIDA (cholescintigraphy)Most accurate for cholecystitis: ~96% sens / ~90% spec. Reserve for equivocal US with ongoing suspicion.Non-visualization of the gallbladder at 60 min = cystic-duct obstruction (positive). Morphine augmentation or 4 h delayed imaging improves specificity; a rim sign suggests gangrene. Requires ~4 h fasting; falsely positive with prolonged fasting/TPN.
CT abdomen/pelvisNot the first test (misses ~⅓ of non-calcified stones) but superb for complications and the septic undifferentiated abdomen.Wall thickening/enhancement, pericholecystic stranding; gas in wall/lumen = emphysematous; discontinuous wall/lack of enhancement = gangrene/perforation; abscess; and it maps CBD dilatation and level of obstruction.
MRCP~90–95% sens / ~95%+ spec for CBD stones; non-invasive road-map of the duct.Best non-invasive test for choledocholithiasis; can miss small stones <6 mm. Use in ASGE intermediate-risk patients to decide who needs ERCP.
EUS~95% sens for CBD stones, superior for small/distal stones; invasive but low-risk.Alternative to MRCP in intermediate risk, especially when MRCP is contraindicated or equivocal; can flow directly into ERCP.
ERCPTherapeutic, not just diagnostic — reserved for high-risk/confirmed CBD stones and cholangitis drainage.Sphincterotomy + stone extraction / stent. Now avoided as a purely diagnostic test because of its ~3–10% pancreatitis and bleeding/perforation risks.
RUQ ultrasound — acute cholecystitis: a thickened gallbladder wall with stones inside casting posterior acoustic shadows. First-line test.
Image: Nevit Dilmen · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Ultrasound — a gallstone (bright echogenic focus) casting a clean posterior acoustic shadow, the sonographic signature of a calculus.
Image: Nevit Dilmen · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Contrast CT — gallstones with a small amount of pericholecystic fluid; CT excels at complications (emphysematous, perforation) and the undifferentiated septic abdomen.
Image: James Heilman, MD · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
HIDA (cholescintigraphy) — tracer excreted into the biliary tree. Non-visualization of the gallbladder at 60 min indicates cystic-duct obstruction (the most accurate test for cholecystitis).
Image: Myohan · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
A negative ultrasound does not exclude cholecystitis. If clinical suspicion is high and the US is equivocal (no wall thickening, no clear stone), the next test is HIDA, not "reassurance." And in the septic patient with an unrevealing US, go to CT to look for emphysematous/gangrenous change or an alternative source.
🧪

Reading the labs — what each value is telling you (and how it lies)

LabWhat it means & why it moves — with confounders
WBC / neutrophilsAcute-phase leukocytosis. In cholecystitis a WBC >18,000/mm³ is a TG18 Grade II marker (think gangrene/perforation). In cholangitis both >12,000 and <4,000 count as abnormal (leukopenia = worse sepsis). A normal WBC never excludes early disease.
CRPRises with inflammatory burden; TG18 uses CRP ≥1 mg/dL as a systemic-inflammation criterion. Nonspecific and lags ~6–12 h behind onset.
Total & direct bilirubinThe pivotal duct marker. Mild rise (<2–4 mg/dL) can occur in cholecystitis (edema/Mirizzi), but a bilirubin ≥2 mg/dL meets the TG18 cholestasis criterion and ≥4 mg/dL with a dilated CBD is an ASGE high-risk predictor of a duct stone. Confounders: Gilbert (unconjugated, benign), hemolysis, sepsis-of-any-cause cholestasis.
ALP & γGTP (GGT)The cholestatic pattern — both rise with ductal obstruction (>1.5× ULN = TG18 criterion). GGT confirms the ALP is biliary (not bone). Rise can lag the obstruction by hours.
AST / ALTUsually mildly up. A transient spike into the hundreds–>1000 U/L that falls fast over 24–48 h is classic for an acute stone passing/impacting the CBD (a brief hepatocellular squeeze) — don't mistake it for viral/ischemic hepatitis.
Lipase / amylaseAlways check — a passing stone can trigger gallstone pancreatitis, which changes management (and lipase >3× ULN with epigastric pain = concurrent pancreatitis).
Blood culturesPositive in a substantial minority of cholecystitis but frequently positive in cholangitis (rising with grade). TG18 recommends cultures in Grade II/III and whenever septic — draw before antibiotics. Also send bile cultures at drainage.
LactateNormal in uncomplicated disease; a rising lactate flags tissue hypoperfusion → the septic-shock (Grade III) pathway and the ICU.
Creatinine / BMP · INR · plateletsNot just chemistry — these are the Grade III organ-dysfunction criteria (Cr >2.0, INR >1.5, platelets <100k). Also needed to dose/renally-adjust antibiotics and to clear coagulopathy before sphincterotomy.
Histopathology — acute cholecystitis: transmural neutrophilic inflammation, mucosal ulceration and wall edema; the tissue correlate of the imaging findings.
Image: Nephron · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

Complications & variants

🧩

The dangerous subtypes — recognize and route each

Variant / complicationHow it shows upManagement thread
Gangrenous cholecystitis (~2–30% of cholecystitis; commonest complication)Higher WBC, older/diabetic/male, less reliable Murphy; wall discontinuity/non-enhancement on CTTG18 Grade II. Urgent cholecystectomy; higher conversion-to-open rate — don't delay.
Emphysematous cholecystitisGas in the gallbladder wall/lumen on imaging; classically diabetic men; Clostridium/E. coliSurgical emergency — high perforation/mortality. Broad antibiotics incl. anaerobes + urgent chole (or cholecystostomy if unfit).
Perforation / empyemaWorsening sepsis, localized then generalized peritonitis; pus-filled GB (empyema)Emergent source control; percutaneous drainage bridge if unfit for OR.
Acalculous cholecystitis (~5–10%, but a big ICU problem)Critically ill, TPN/fasting, on vasopressors/ventilator; unexplained sepsis + RUQ US changes, no stonesIschemia/stasis-driven. Percutaneous cholecystostomy is first-line; interval cholecystectomy often unnecessary if no stones.
Mirizzi syndromeStone in cystic duct/Hartmann's pouch extrinsically compresses the CBD → obstructive jaundice mimicking a duct stoneMRCP to define; surgically challenging (higher bile-duct-injury risk) — flag the surgeon pre-op.
Gallstone ileus / BouveretLarge stone erodes through into bowel via a cholecystoenteric fistula → mechanical obstruction (ileus at ileocecal valve; Bouveret = duodenal)Look for pneumobilia + SBO + ectopic stone (Rigler triad); surgical.
Cholangitis with abscess / thrombophlebitisPersistent sepsis after drainage; hepatic abscesses, portal pyemiaSource control + prolonged antibiotics; drain abscesses.
Gallstone pancreatitisConcurrent epigastric pain, lipase >3× ULN — a stone at/through the ampullaManaged as pancreatitis; urgent ERCP only if concurrent cholangitis or persistent obstruction (see APEC).
The variants that can't wait: emphysematous cholecystitis (gas in the wall), gangrenous/perforated gallbladder, and any cholangitis with hypotension or confusion (Reynolds). These skip the "observe and re-image" pathway and go straight to urgent source control ± ICU.

Assess

Recognizing it in clinic

🔍

Biliary colic vs cholecystitis vs "get to the ED"

Most gallstone disease reaches you as biliary colic: episodic, dull RUQ/epigastric pain that builds over an hour, plateaus, and resolves within <6 hours — the gallbladder contracting against a transiently obstructing stone that then falls back. It is often postprandial (fatty meals) and the patient is well between attacks with a normal exam and normal labs. That is a clinic problem: confirm stones on ultrasound and refer for elective cholecystectomy.

The moment the pain becomes constant and lasts >5–6 hours, or the patient develops fever, a positive Murphy's sign, or looks unwell, the diagnosis has shifted to acute cholecystitis — that is an ED/admission problem, not a clinic follow-up. And any jaundice, dark urine, or rigors raises choledocholithiasis/cholangitis, which needs same-day evaluation.

Who is at risk (the classic "5 F's" — female, forty, fertile, fat, fair, plus rapid weight loss, family history, Native American ancestry, TPN, ceftriaxone, octreotide, estrogen/OCPs, and hemolytic disease for pigment stones). ~10–15% of adults have gallstones; only ~1–4%/yr of those become symptomatic, and only a fraction of symptomatic patients progress to cholecystitis.

"Biliary colic" is a misnomer — the pain is a steady crescendo–plateau, not a colicky wax-and-wane. If a patient describes truly intermittent 10-minute spasms, rethink the diagnosis (renal colic, bowel).

Outpatient management — first-line → escalation

💊

Biliary colic & the gallstone decision

the definitive fix is surgical
1
Acute biliary-colic attack — analgesia
NSAIDs are first-line and may reduce progression to cholecystitis
▾
The pain of biliary colic is driven by prostaglandin-mediated gallbladder wall tension against an obstructing stone. NSAIDs block that prostaglandin synthesis — they relieve pain and, in a landmark RCT (Akriviadis 1997), reduced progression of biliary colic to acute cholecystitis. Prefer them over opioids.
DrugStart doseTitration / maxWhy it works / roleIf contraindicated / alt
Diclofenac (evidence-based)75 mg IM ×1May repeat; max 150 mg/dayThe agent in Akriviadis 1997 — reduced progression to cholecystitis. NSAID = blocks prostaglandin-driven wall tension.CKD/PUD/CHF → acetaminophen; opioid if truly refractory
Ketorolac30 mg IV / 60 mg IM ×1 (15 mg IV if >65 y or <50 kg)15–30 mg IV q6h, max 5 days, ≤120 mg/day (60 mg/day if elderly/renal)Potent parenteral NSAID for the ED/urgent visit; same mechanism.Renal impairment, bleeding risk → avoid; use acetaminophen
Ibuprofen / naproxen (oral)Ibuprofen 400–600 mg POq6–8h PRN, max 2.4 g/dayOral option for milder attacks at home.GI/renal risk → acetaminophen 1 g q6h
Acetaminophen1000 mg PO/IVq6h, max 3–4 g/dayAdjunct / NSAID-sparing when NSAIDs are contraindicated.Hepatic dysfunction → reduce max
Opioid (e.g., morphine, hydromorphone)Morphine 2–4 mg IVtitrate PRN severe painReserve for severe pain unrelieved by NSAIDs. The old "morphine causes sphincter-of-Oddi spasm, use meperidine" teaching is a myth — meperidine has no proven advantage and worse side effects.Hydromorphone 0.2–0.5 mg IV as alternative
2
Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy — the definitive treatment
For symptomatic gallstones; refer after the first genuine biliary episode
▾

Symptomatic gallstones recur (~⅔ within 2 years) and carry an ongoing risk of cholecystitis, cholangitis, and pancreatitis. Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment and is recommended after the first clear symptomatic episode in a fit patient. It removes the organ that makes and traps stones — there is no medical equivalent.

Prophylactic cholecystectomy for ASYMPTOMATIC stones is not routine, but is indicated for higher-cancer/complication-risk situations: porcelain gallbladder, gallstones >3 cm, gallbladder polyps >10 mm (or growing), anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction, patients with hemolytic anemia (e.g., sickle cell) undergoing splenectomy, and some transplant candidates / select Indigenous populations at high gallbladder-cancer risk.
3
Non-operative / dissolution options — limited niche
When surgery is refused or deferred
▾
OptionDoseWho it (rarely) helpsWhy it usually fails
Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)8–10 mg/kg/day PO divided (dissolution); ~300 mg BID prophylaxisSmall (<5–10 mm) radiolucent cholesterol stones in a functioning gallbladder; a non-surgical patientTakes 6–24 months, works in a minority, and stones recur in ~50% once stopped — so it is not a substitute for surgery.
UDCA for prophylaxis in rapid weight loss~500–600 mg/day during active lossBariatric surgery / very-low-calorie diets (reduces new stone formation)Preventive only; doesn't clear existing stones.
Dietary modificationReduce dietary fat; weight loss (gradual)Reduces attack frequencyDoes not dissolve stones or replace cholecystectomy.
Trying to manage recurrent symptomatic gallstones with UDCA instead of surgery is like repeatedly bailing water out of a boat with a hole in it — you can slow the flooding, but until you take out the leaking hull (the gallbladder), the problem keeps coming back.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How the common comorbidities change the course and the plan

ComorbidityEffect on diseaseWhat it changes in management
Diabetes mellitusHigher rate of emphysematous & gangrenous cholecystitis; blunted symptoms; worse outcomesDo not delay — low threshold to image, admit, and operate; broad antibiotics with anaerobic cover; tight glucose control.
Cirrhosis / portal hypertensionCholecystectomy carries much higher mortality (rises with Child class); coagulopathy, varices at the portaPrefer subtotal cholecystectomy or cholecystostomy in decompensated patients; correct coagulopathy; involve hepatobiliary surgery early.
PregnancyGallstones common (estrogen, stasis); can present atypicallyLaparoscopic cholecystectomy is safe, ideally 2nd trimester (SAGES); US/MRCP for imaging (no CT); ERCP with abdominal shielding if needed; avoid fluoroquinolones.
Elderly / frailtyAtypical/muted presentation, higher gangrene & mortality; comorbidity index drives operative riskTG18 uses comorbidity (CCI) & performance status to pick surgery vs cholecystostomy in Grade II/III; individualize.
CKDAlters antibiotic clearance; contrast & NSAID cautionRenally dose β-lactams/fluoroquinolones; avoid NSAIDs and aminoglycosides; hydrate for contrast.
Post-bariatric / Roux-en-Y anatomyRapid weight loss → stones; and conventional ERCP is impossible through altered anatomyFor a CBD stone → laparoscopy-assisted (transgastric) ERCP or EUS-directed drainage; plan ahead with advanced endoscopy.
Anticoagulation / antiplateletsBleeding risk with sphincterotomy & percutaneous drainageHold per ASGE peri-endoscopic guidance (warfarin/DOAC timing); sphincterotomy is high-bleeding-risk — plan interruption/bridging.
Hemolytic disease (sickle cell, spherocytosis)Chronic hemolysis → pigment (bilirubin) stones from young ageProphylactic cholecystectomy often bundled with splenectomy; keep biliary disease on the differential in any crisis with RUQ pain.
Drugs to avoid / use with caution: Ceftriaxone (causes biliary pseudolithiasis/sludge that mimics stones — usually reversible; avoid or switch if it appears). Estrogens/OCPs, fibrates, octreotide, and GLP-1 agonists / rapid weight loss all promote stone formation. Aminoglycosides add nephrotoxicity when contrast and sepsis already threaten the kidney. NSAIDs are first-line for colic but avoid in CKD, active PUD, or heart failure. And the classic pitfall — don't withhold morphine over the sphincter-of-Oddi myth; treat the pain.

Does this patient have a duct stone? (ASGE 2019)

🧮

ASGE choledocholithiasis risk stratifier

decides ERCP vs MRCP/EUS vs straight-to-surgery

Before cholecystectomy, this ASGE 2019 tool (Buxbaum) answers "who needs their common bile duct cleared first." Select every feature present — the calculator returns the highest risk tier and its pathway.

High-risk predictors (any one → high)

CBD stone seen on US / cross-sectional imaging High
Clinical ascending cholangitis High
Total bilirubin >4 mg/dL and dilated CBD (>6 mm, GB in situ) High

Intermediate-risk predictors (any one → intermediate)

Abnormal liver biochemical test (not meeting high) Int
Age >55 years Int
Dilated CBD on imaging (>6 mm) Int
Low risk
No predictors selected — low risk (<10%). Proceed to cholecystectomy without further duct evaluation (intra-op cholangiogram at the surgeon's discretion).

Risk bands: high >50%, intermediate 10–50%, low <10% probability of a CBD stone (ASGE 2019). See also the TG18 diagnostic/severity calculators in Wards (cholecystitis) and ICU (cholangitis).

Prevent

USPSTF A/B & whole-patient prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B screening relevant to this patient

There is no USPSTF recommendation to screen for gallstones or gallbladder cancer — asymptomatic stones are common and usually benign, so screening isn't indicated. The high-yield prevention here is treating the metabolic risk factors that both cause gallstones and raise perioperative risk.

GradeRecommendationPopulation
BIntensive behavioral intervention for obesity (a core gallstone risk factor)Adults with BMI ≥30
BHealthy diet & physical activity counseling to prevent CVDAdults with cardiometabolic risk factors
ATobacco cessation — ask + advise + pharmacotherapy (also reduces peri-op complications)All adults who use tobacco
BUnhealthy alcohol use screening + brief counselingAdults ≥18 y
BPrediabetes/type 2 diabetes screeningAdults 35–70 y with overweight/obesity
BStatin for primary prevention when 10-yr CVD risk ≥10% (peri-op optimization)Adults 40–75 y with ≥1 risk factor
Counsel that gradual weight loss (not crash diets) lowers gallstone risk — rapid weight loss and very-low-calorie diets cause stones, which is why UDCA prophylaxis is offered around bariatric surgery.
Escalate

When clinic isn't enough

🚑

Red flags → ED / same-day admission

Send to the ED now for any of: constant RUQ pain >5–6 h with a positive Murphy's sign · fever/rigors · jaundice, dark urine, or pale stools (duct obstruction) · the Charcot triad (fever + RUQ pain + jaundice → cholangitis) · hypotension or confusion (Reynolds pentad → septic shock) · intractable vomiting/dehydration · or epigastric pain with vomiting suggesting gallstone pancreatitis. Cholangitis and complicated cholecystitis are time-sensitive — the delay to drainage is what kills.
🛏️ Wards — admit, antibiotics, and the timing of source control
Admit

Who gets admitted & the TG18 grade

📋

Admission criteria

Essentially all acute cholecystitis and all acute cholangitis are admitted — both need IV antibiotics, NPO, analgesia, and a plan for source control. Admit for any of:

  • Confirmed acute cholecystitis (TG18) — for antibiotics and cholecystectomy planning.
  • Any acute cholangitis — this is a drainage emergency; never manage as an outpatient.
  • Systemic illness — SIRS/sepsis, high fever, rigors, hypotension, or a toxic appearance.
  • Complicated cholecystitis — gangrenous, emphysematous, perforated, empyema, or abscess.
  • Can't tolerate oral / uncontrolled pain / dehydration.
  • Concurrent gallstone pancreatitis or a suspected CBD stone needing ERCP.
  • High-risk host — diabetes, immunosuppression, cirrhosis, elderly/frail.
The first job on admission is to assign the TG18 grade — it sets the urgency of drainage/surgery, the antibiotic breadth, and the level of care. Grade the cholecystitis with the calculator below; grade cholangitis in the ICU tab.
🧮

TG18 acute cholecystitis severity grade

drives timing & disposition

Select every feature present. Grade III (any organ dysfunction) overrides; otherwise any one Grade II feature = moderate; none = mild.

Grade III — organ dysfunction (any one)

Cardiovascular — hypotension needing dopamine ≥5 µg/kg/min or any norepinephrine III
Neurological — decreased consciousness III
Respiratory — PaO₂/FiO₂ <300 III
Renal — oliguria or creatinine >2.0 mg/dL III
Hepatic — PT-INR >1.5 III
Hematological — platelets <100,000/mm³ III

Grade II — marked local inflammation (any one)

WBC >18,000/mm³ II
Palpable tender RUQ mass II
Duration >72 h II
Marked inflammation (gangrene, emphysema, abscess, biliary peritonitis) II
Grade I — Mild
No Grade II/III features selected — mild. Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (ideally <72 h) + antibiotics; manage on the floor.

Treat

Acute inpatient therapy

💊

Empiric antibiotics — TG18 by severity grade

GNR + anaerobe ± Enterococcus
Target the translocated biliary flora — E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter (gram-negatives), Enterococcus, and anaerobes (esp. Bacteroides). Breadth scales with severity and healthcare exposure. TG18 note: ampicillin-sulbactam is no longer recommended because >20% of E. coli are now resistant. Add metronidazole for anaerobes when a bilioenteric anastomosis or Grade III disease is present (cephalosporins except cefoxitin/cefmetazole lack anaerobic cover). Cover Enterococcus in healthcare-associated infection, Grade III, immunocompromise, prior biliary instrumentation/stent, or when it grows.

Duration & de-escalationCholecystitis: after cholecystectomy for Grade I–mild disease, no post-op antibiotics are needed (Regimbeau JAMA 2014) — or stop within 24 h. Gangrenous/perforated/emphysematous → 4–7 days after source control. Cholangitis: continue 4–7 days after adequate biliary drainage; if gram-positive bacteremia (Enterococcus/Streptococcus) → treat ~2 weeks (endocarditis risk). Always de-escalate to culture-directed therapy and switch IV→PO once afebrile and improving.
🔪

Source control — the definitive move for each disease

DiseaseDefinitive procedureTiming (guideline)
Acute cholecystitis (fit patient)Early laparoscopic cholecystectomyWithin 72 h of onset ideally (WSES 2020 / TG18); early beats delayed (ACDC, Gurusamy Cochrane — fewer complications, shorter stay). Up to ~7–10 days acceptable at experienced centers.
Cholecystitis, high surgical risk / Grade III unfitPercutaneous cholecystostomy (drain) as a bridgeWhen too unstable/comorbid for immediate surgery; interval cholecystectomy later. (CHOCOLATE favored surgery when feasible.)
Acute cholangitisBiliary drainage — ERCP with sphincterotomy + stone extraction / stentGrade I: antibiotics; drain if no response in 24 h. Grade II: early drainage (≤48 h). Grade III: urgent drainage as soon as stabilized. (Lai 1992: endoscopic drainage halved mortality vs surgery.)
Cholangitis, ERCP failed / altered anatomyPTBD (percutaneous transhepatic) or EUS-guided drainageWhen ERCP fails or Roux-en-Y/gastric bypass makes it impossible.
ERCP — a filling defect (arrow) from a stone impacted in the distal CBD. Sphincterotomy + extraction both relieves the pressure driving cholangitis and removes the stone.
Image: Samir · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
MRCP — stones in the gallbladder and common bile duct. The non-invasive duct map used to triage ASGE intermediate-risk patients before ERCP.
Image: Hellerhoff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Post-ERCP pancreatitis prophylaxis: give rectal indomethacin 100 mg PR immediately after ERCP in patients at risk (Elmunzer NEJM 2012 reduced post-ERCP pancreatitis; NNT ≈ 13–17). Prophylactic pancreatic-duct stents help in selected high-risk cases.
Sequence for a CBD stone with the gallbladder still in: ERCP to clear the duct first, then cholecystectomy (often same admission). Don't send a patient home with a cleared duct but a stone-filled gallbladder — recurrence is high.
💉

Supportive care

  • Analgesia: ketorolac 15–30 mg IV q6h (≤5 days, avoid in CKD/PUD/CHF) or opioids (morphine 2–4 mg IV q3–4h / hydromorphone 0.2–0.5 mg IV). Treat the pain — the sphincter-of-Oddi/morphine concern is a myth.
  • Antiemetics: ondansetron 4 mg IV q6–8h PRN.
  • Fluids/electrolytes: replace deficits; correct K⁺/Mg²⁺ (esp. if QT-prolonging antibiotics).
  • Coagulopathy: vitamin K / reverse anticoagulation before sphincterotomy (high-bleeding-risk procedure).
Monitor

What to trend each day

📈

Daily assessment

  • Vitals & perfusion: defervescence, resolution of tachycardia, MAP, urine output — new instability = re-grade and escalate.
  • Exam: RUQ tenderness improving vs spreading (peritonism = complication).
  • Labs: WBC/CRP down-trending; bilirubin & LFTs falling after drainage confirms the duct is decompressed; lactate if any concern; INR/plts/Cr for organ function.
  • Post-drainage: for cholangitis, clinical + biochemical response within 24–48 h of ERCP is expected; failure to improve → repeat imaging / re-drain / look for abscess.
  • Cholecystostomy tube: output and character; plan a clamp trial then cholangiogram before removal (see ICU).
The 48-hour rule: a cholangitis patient whose fever, pain, or bilirubin is not clearly improving 24–48 h after drainage has an inadequately decompressed or re-obstructed duct, an undrained abscess, or the wrong bug — image and reintervene rather than just waiting.
Escalate

When to call the ICU / urgent drainage

⬆️

Concrete escalation triggers

Transfer to a higher level of care / call for emergent drainage for any of:
  • Hemodynamics: SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 despite a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus → vasopressor need = ICU (TG18 Grade III).
  • Perfusion: lactate >2 mmol/L and rising (≥4 = overt shock); new oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h); mottling.
  • Organ dysfunction: new confusion, PaO₂/FiO₂ <300, creatinine >2.0, INR >1.5, platelets <100k — any one is Grade III.
  • Cholangitis not responding to antibiotics → needs urgent biliary drainage now, not tomorrow.
  • Complicated cholecystitis — emphysematous/perforation/peritonitis → emergent surgery.

qSOFA — quick bedside sepsis screen (1 point each):

Respiratory rate ≥22 /min +1
Systolic BP ≤100 mmHg +1
Altered mentation (GCS <15) +1
0
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: afebrile ~24 h · hemodynamically stable · pain controlled on oral analgesia · tolerating diet · WBC/CRP and (for cholangitis) bilirubin trending down after drainage · source control achieved or clearly scheduled (cholecystectomy date; ERCP done) · any drain/tube plan in place.

Home

Most patients post-cholecystectomy or post-ERCP — recovered, independent, with a clear follow-up and (if GB still in) an interval cholecystectomy date.

Home health

Home with a cholecystostomy tube or completing IV/OPAT antibiotics; wound/tube nursing.

SNF

Deconditioned elderly / post-op patient needing 24-h skilled nursing but <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Post-op patient able to tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged complex recovery — e.g., open abdomen, prolonged ventilation after severe biliary sepsis.

Hospice / palliative

Frail patient with malignant obstruction not a drainage/surgical candidate, or comfort-focused goals.
Interval cholecystectomy after cholangitis: once the duct is cleared, a patient whose gallbladder still holds stones remains at high risk of recurrent cholangitis/cholecystitis — schedule cholecystectomy (same admission if fit, or after recovery). A patient who had a cholecystostomy tube needs a tube-management plan (clamp trial + cholangiogram before removal) and interval surgery if calculous.
🫀 ICU — biliary sepsis, septic shock & emergent decompression
Admit

ICU triggers & the TG18 cholangitis grade

🚨

When biliary disease belongs in the unit

Biliary sepsis reaches the ICU as TG18 Grade III — cholecystitis or cholangitis with organ dysfunction — or as septic shock from cholangiovenous bacteremia. The unifying driver is an undrained, pressurized, infected biliary system seeding the blood; the ICU stabilizes the patient so that emergent drainage can happen, because antibiotics + pressors alone will not reverse an obstructed duct.

  • Septic shock — hypotension needing vasopressors after fluids; lactate ≥2 (≥4 = overt).
  • Any TG18 Grade III organ dysfunction — cardiovascular, neurological, respiratory (P/F <300), renal (Cr >2.0), hepatic (INR >1.5), hematological (plts <100k).
  • Reynolds pentad (Charcot + hypotension + confusion) — severe cholangitis.
  • Emphysematous/gangrenous/perforated cholecystitis needing emergent surgery + support.
  • Peri-procedural instability — before/after urgent ERCP or surgery.
🧮

TG18 acute cholangitis severity grade

sets drainage urgency

Grade III (any organ dysfunction) overrides. Otherwise any TWO Grade II features = moderate; fewer than two = mild.

Grade III — organ dysfunction (any one)

Cardiovascular — dopamine ≥5 µg/kg/min or any norepinephrine III
Neurological — disturbance of consciousness III
Respiratory — PaO₂/FiO₂ <300 III
Renal — oliguria or creatinine >2.0 mg/dL III
Hepatic — PT-INR >1.5 III
Hematological — platelets <100,000/mm³ III

Grade II — need any TWO

WBC >12,000 or <4,000/mm³ II
Fever ≥39 °C II
Age ≥75 years II
Total bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL II
Albumin <0.7× lower limit of normal II
Grade I — Mild
Fewer than two Grade II features and no organ dysfunction — mild. Antibiotics + supportive care; biliary drainage if no response within 24 h.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Access: central line for vasopressors + CVP trend; arterial line for beat-to-beat MAP and frequent lactate/ABG draws; large-bore IV for resuscitation.
  • Resuscitation targets (Surviving Sepsis 2021): MAP ≥65 mmHg; normalize/clear lactate; urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h; give 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension/lactate ≥4, then dynamic fluid-responsiveness assessment.
  • Trend: lactate q2–6h during resuscitation; CBC, CMP, LFTs/bilirubin, INR, blood + bile cultures; and the organ-dysfunction panel that defines Grade III.
  • Source assessment: confirm the duct is drained (falling bilirubin after ERCP) — persistent sepsis with a rising bilirubin means the source is still uncontrolled.
Support

Pressors, inotropes & antibiotics in biliary septic shock

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 ≫ β1Start 0.05 µg/kg/min; titrate to MAP ≥65; usual 0.05–0.5 (max ~1) µg/kg/min↑↑ SVR, mild ↑ COFirst-line vasopressor in septic shock (SSC 2021)
VasopressinV1 vascular receptorsFixed 0.03 U/min (not titrated)↑ SVR, catecholamine-sparingAdd when norepi ~0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min to reach MAP / lower norepi dose
Epinephrineβ1, β2, α10.01–0.5 µg/kg/min↑ CO + ↑ SVR (↑ lactate)Second/third-line add-on for refractory shock
Dobutamineβ1 > β2 (inotrope)2.5–20 µg/kg/min↑ contractility/CO, may ↓ SVRAdd if septic cardiomyopathy / persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate MAP
HydrocortisoneGlucocorticoid (vascular tone)50 mg IV q6h (or 200 mg/day infusion)Restores catecholamine responsivenessRefractory shock on escalating vasopressors (SSC 2021)
Distributive (vasodilatory) shock from endotoxemia is a low-SVR state, so the goal is to restore vascular tone — hence an α1-dominant agent (norepinephrine) first. Vasopressin adds a non-catecholamine vasoconstrictor to spare high norepi doses. Dobutamine is added only when the problem is pump failure (septic cardiomyopathy), not tone. None of this substitutes for drainage — the vasopressor requirement keeps climbing until the biliary source is decompressed.
Antibiotics in the unitGive broad empiric cover within 1 hour (Surviving Sepsis) after blood cultures: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h or meropenem 1 g IV q8h for healthcare-associated/prior-stent, + vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg for Enterococcus/MRSA risk, ± an echinocandin if Candida is likely. De-escalate on cultures; source control is the definitive therapy.
Source control

Emergent biliary decompression

⚙️

Drain the tree — the intervention that saves the patient

In Grade III cholangitis, mortality tracks with time to drainage. Stabilize and decompress — do not delay drainage waiting for the patient to be "optimized," because the sepsis will not resolve until the pressure is relieved.

ModalityRole / whenNotes
ERCP + sphincterotomy / stent (first-line)Emergent decompression of the obstructed CBD once stabilized; can be done under GA in the intubated patientEndoscopic drainage halved mortality vs open surgery (Lai 1992). A stent alone (without stone extraction) is a valid "drain now, clear later" strategy in the unstable.
PTBD (percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage)When ERCP fails, is unavailable, or anatomy (Roux-en-Y) precludes itIR-placed external/internal drain; useful bridge in the crashing patient.
EUS-guided biliary drainageAt advanced centers when ERCP failsEmerging alternative to PTBD.
Percutaneous cholecystostomyGrade III / high-risk cholecystitis unfit for surgery; and acalculous cholecystitisBedside/IR drain decompresses the gallbladder; interval cholecystectomy later if calculous.
Open/lap cholecystectomy or CBD explorationWhen endoscopic/percutaneous options failHigher risk in the septic, coagulopathic patient — a last resort for drainage.
Acalculous cholecystitis — suspect it in any ICU patient with unexplained sepsis, especially on TPN, fasting, vasopressors, or a ventilator. US shows a distended, thick-walled gallbladder with sludge and pericholecystic fluid but no stones. First-line treatment is percutaneous cholecystostomy (most are too unstable for surgery); because there are no stones, interval cholecystectomy is often unnecessary once recovered.
Cholecystostomy tube management: leave it to gravity drainage; once the patient recovers, do a clamp trial, then a tube cholangiogram to confirm cystic-duct patency and no residual CBD stone before removal — and allow ~3–6 weeks for the tract to mature so bile doesn't leak into the peritoneum on removal.
Airway

Respiratory support

🌬️

Intubation for sepsis / peri-procedural, lung-protective settings

Intubation is driven by the sepsis (obtundation/airway protection, shock work of breathing, ARDS) or to safely perform emergent ERCP/surgery in an unstable patient — not by the biliary disease itself. Use lung-protective ventilation; if sepsis-induced ARDS develops, follow ARDSNet.

Downgrade

When to step down

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: source controlled (duct drained / gallbladder removed or drained) · off vasopressors ≥6–24 h with MAP ≥65 · lactate cleared · improving mentation · bilirubin/LFTs and WBC trending down · extubated or stable on minimal support · resolving AKI/coagulopathy. Not yet if the patient still needs pressors, the biliary source remains undrained, or the lactate/bilirubin is still climbing — that means the source isn't controlled.

ICU disposition: most recover and step down to the floor for antibiotic completion and interval cholecystectomy planning. The frail patient with malignant obstruction or recurrent biliary sepsis who is not a drainage/surgical candidate warrants an early goals-of-care conversation and palliative input.

Shared

Pearls & pitfalls

💡

The high-yield, practice-changing points

  1. Fever is present in only ~⅓ of acute cholecystitis — its absence never excludes it (early disease is a chemical inflammation). A high fever/rigors should make you think secondary infection, gangrene, or actually cholangitis. (Trowbridge, JAMA 2003)
  2. No single sign or lab rules cholecystitis in or out. Even Murphy's sign has an LR+ whose confidence interval crosses 1 — diagnosis rests on clinical gestalt + ultrasound, not any one finding.
  3. A transient AST/ALT spike into the hundreds–>1000 that falls fast over 24–48 h = a stone that passed through the CBD, not primary hepatitis. Seen in ~6% of choledocholithiasis.
  4. A negative ultrasound does not exclude cholecystitis. If suspicion persists (especially acalculous in the ICU), the next test is HIDA (~96% sensitive), not reassurance.
  5. In septic cholangitis, don't wait for MRCP. Resuscitate and get urgent ERCP/drainage — drainage within 24 h lowers mortality. MRCP is for stable intermediate-risk triage, not the crashing patient.
  6. Charcot triad is specific (~96%) but insensitive (~26%). Most cholangitis presents incomplete — use the TG18 criteria, which are far more sensitive, and keep cholangitis on the list for any gram-negative bacteremia.
  7. Cholangitis can occur without jaundice — classically with a partially occluded biliary stent, and a normal-caliber duct early doesn't exclude it (the stone can obstruct before the duct dilates).
  8. Add enterococcal coverage (vancomycin) after prior ERCP/stent, or in Grade III / healthcare-associated disease — enterococci colonize instrumented ducts and pip-tazo/carbapenems don't reliably cover E. faecium.
  9. Stop antibiotics ~24 h after cholecystectomy for mild/moderate cholecystitis — continuing adds nothing (Regimbeau, JAMA 2014).
  10. Give rectal indomethacin 100 mg to high-risk ERCP patients — NNT ≈ 13 to prevent post-ERCP pancreatitis (Elmunzer, NEJM 2012).
  11. Clamp the cholecystostomy tube (~48 h) and get a cholangiogram before removal, and let the tract mature ~2–3 weeks — pull it early and bile leaks into the peritoneum.
  12. Ceftriaxone causes biliary sludge/pseudolithiasis that mimics stones and reverses when you stop the drug — don't rush an incidental "stone" to surgery in a patient on ceftriaxone.
  13. HIDA needs ~4 h of fasting (a recently fed, contracted gallbladder gives a false non-fill); morphine augmentation improves specificity, but prolonged fasting/TPN causes false positives.
  14. Don't delay source control in diabetics — emphysematous and gangrenous cholecystitis develop fast and carry high perforation/mortality.
  15. No urgent ERCP for gallstone pancreatitis unless there is concurrent cholangitis or ongoing obstruction (APEC) — the benefit is in the cholangitis subgroup, not routine biliary pancreatitis.
  16. The morphine / sphincter-of-Oddi rule is a myth — opioids are not contraindicated in biliary disease; treat the pain and don't reach for meperidine.

Educational reference for an incoming IM resident. Verify every dose against your institution's formulary and the current guideline before acting on any individual patient. Guideline positions reflect Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18), WSES 2020, ASGE 2019, ACR Appropriateness Criteria 2022, IDSA/SIS intra-abdominal infection guidance, and Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021. TG18 lists antibiotic agents by severity grade; milligram doses shown are standard adult IV doses (IDSA/reference) matched to those agents and always require renal adjustment.
